questions.q: Which of these is a point-to-point link rather than a broadcast (shared-medium) link?
choices: 802.11 wireless LAN
Upstream HFC in a cable-based access network
The link between an Ethernet switch and a host
A shared satellite radio channel
questions.explain: A switch-to-host Ethernet link (and PPP for dial-up) has exactly one sender and one receiver at each end. Old-school shared Ethernet, upstream HFC, 802.11, 4G/5G and satellite are all broadcast media.

questions.q: On a shared broadcast channel, a collision occurs when a node receives two or more signals at the same time.
questions.explain: Two or more simultaneous transmissions interfere. A node that receives overlapping signals cannot decode any of them, and that is a collision.

questions.q: Multiple access protocols usually coordinate channel sharing over a separate out-of-band control channel.
questions.explain: There is no out-of-band channel. Any communication about who may transmit has to use the same shared channel being coordinated.

questions.q: Given a multiple access channel of rate R bps, which of these are properties of an ideal multiple access protocol?
choices: When one node wants to transmit, it can send at rate R
When M nodes want to transmit, each can send at an average rate of R/M
Fully decentralized: no special node coordinates transmissions
No synchronization of clocks or slots is needed
Each of the N attached nodes always gets exactly R/N, even when it is the only active node
A central master detects collisions and tells nodes when to retransmit
questions.explain: The ideal is: full rate R for a lone sender, a fair R/M share among M active senders, full decentralization (no master, no clock or slot sync), and simplicity. A fixed R/N share regardless of load is how channel partitioning falls short. A central master goes against decentralization.

questions.q: An ideal multiple access protocol runs on a 100 Mbps channel. If 4 nodes want to transmit at once, what average rate (in Mbps) should each one get?
questions.explain: Ideally each of M active nodes gets R/M = 100/4 = 25 Mbps.

questions.q: Which class of MAC protocol divides the channel into smaller pieces (time slots, frequencies or codes) and gives each piece to one node for its exclusive use?
choices: Random access
Channel partitioning
Taking turns
Carrier sensing
questions.explain: Channel partitioning (TDMA, FDMA, or division by code) splits the channel up and allocates each piece exclusively.

questions.q: Which class of MAC protocol leaves the channel undivided, allows collisions, and then recovers from them?
choices: Channel partitioning
Taking turns
Random access
Polling
questions.explain: Random access protocols (ALOHA, slotted ALOHA, CSMA, CSMA/CD, CSMA/CA) send at the full rate with no prior coordination, accept collisions, and say how to detect them and recover.

questions.q: Which wireless LAN uses CSMA/CA (collision avoidance) as its MAC protocol?
choices: Ethernet
Bluetooth
Token ring
questions.explain: CSMA/CA is used in 802.11. Ethernet uses CSMA/CD. Bluetooth (polling) and token ring are taking-turns protocols.

questions.q: In TDMA, what happens to a station's time slot in a round when that station has nothing to send?
choices: It is given to the next station that has a packet
Stations with packets contend for it at random
The round is shortened to skip it
It goes idle
questions.explain: Each station owns a fixed-length slot in every round. Unused slots go idle and are not handed to anyone else.

questions.q: In TDMA, how long is each station's slot?
choices: One packet transmission time
One round-trip propagation delay
512 bit times
It varies with how much the station has queued
questions.explain: Each station gets a fixed-length slot per round, and the slot length equals the time to transmit one packet.

questions.q: A 6-station LAN uses TDMA with 6-slot frames. Only stations 1, 3 and 4 have packets to send. What fraction of the slots in each frame carry data? (Give a decimal.)
questions.explain: Slots 1, 3 and 4 are used, and slots 2, 5 and 6 go idle. That is 3 of 6, or 0.5.

questions.q: In FDMA, what does each station get?
choices: A fixed time slot in each round
A fixed frequency band of the channel spectrum
A token that lets it transmit
The full channel whenever it senses the channel idle
questions.explain: FDMA divides the channel spectrum into frequency bands and gives each station a fixed band. Transmission time in unused bands goes idle.

questions.q: A 60 Mbps channel is shared by 6 stations using TDMA. Only one station is active. What throughput (in Mbps) does it get?
questions.explain: Channel partitioning gives each node 1/N of the bandwidth even when it is the only active node: 60/6 = 10 Mbps. The other slots go idle.

questions.q: What is the main weakness of channel partitioning MAC protocols?
choices: They waste capacity on collisions at high load
They are unfair when every node has data to send
They are inefficient at low load: nodes wait for their piece and get only 1/N of the bandwidth even if they are the only active node
They need a central controller to poll each node
questions.explain: Partitioning shares the channel efficiently and fairly at high load. At low load it delays channel access and caps a lone active node at 1/N of the bandwidth.

questions.q: Which of these are assumptions of slotted ALOHA?
choices: All frames are the same size
Time is divided into equal slots, each the time to transmit one frame
Nodes start transmitting only at the beginning of a slot
Nodes are synchronized
If two or more nodes transmit in a slot, all nodes detect the collision
Nodes sense the channel before transmitting and defer if it is busy
A central node assigns slots to nodes
questions.explain: Slotted ALOHA assumes equal-size frames, slots one frame-time long, transmissions only at slot starts, synchronized nodes, and collision detection by all nodes. It does no carrier sensing (that is CSMA) and has no central assigner.

questions.q: In slotted ALOHA, what does a node do after its frame collides?
choices: Retransmits in the very next slot
Waits K·512 bit times, with K chosen from {0, ..., 2^m − 1}
Waits for the channel to be sensed idle, then retransmits
Retransmits the frame in each later slot with probability p until it succeeds
questions.explain: After a collision the node retransmits in each later slot with probability p until it succeeds. With no collision, it can send a new frame in the next slot.

questions.q: Why does slotted ALOHA retransmit with probability p after a collision, instead of always retransmitting in the next slot?
choices: If every colliding node retransmitted right away, they would collide again in every later slot
It lets nodes skip clock synchronization
It makes all frames the same size
It lets a central node choose who goes next
questions.explain: Colliding nodes that always retransmitted in the next slot would keep colliding with each other. Random choices break the symmetry, so eventually only one of them transmits in a slot.

questions.q: In slotted ALOHA, N = 3 nodes always have frames to send, and each transmits in a slot with probability p = 0.5. What is the probability that one particular node succeeds in a given slot?
questions.explain: A given node succeeds with probability p(1−p)^(N−1) = 0.5 × 0.5^2 = 0.125. It must transmit, and the other N−1 nodes must not.

questions.q: In slotted ALOHA, N = 4 nodes always have frames to send, and each transmits in a slot with probability p = 0.25. What is the probability that some node succeeds in a given slot?
As the number of nodes N goes to infinity, what is the maximum efficiency of slotted ALOHA?
choices: 1, since a single node can use the full rate
questions.explain: Maximizing Np(1−p)^(N−1) and letting N go to infinity gives 1/e ≈ 0.37. At best, the channel carries useful transmissions only 37% of the time.

questions.q: How is the efficiency of slotted ALOHA defined?
choices: The fraction of time a single active node can transmit
The ratio of propagation delay to frame transmission time
The long-run fraction of successful slots when there are many nodes, all with many frames to send
The fraction of slots that are empty
questions.explain: Efficiency is the long-run fraction of slots that carry a successful transmission, measured under heavy load (many nodes, each with many frames).

questions.q: For N nodes that each transmit with probability p, what value p* maximizes the slotted ALOHA success probability Np(1−p)^(N−1)?
questions.explain: Set the derivative N(1−p)^(N−2)[(1−p) − (N−1)p] to zero. This gives 1 − Np = 0, so p* = 1/N. Plugging in and letting N go to infinity gives the 1/e limit.

questions.q: Which of these are drawbacks of slotted ALOHA?
choices: Collisions waste slots
Some slots go idle
Nodes may be able to detect a collision before finishing the frame, but still use the whole slot
Nodes need clock synchronization
A single active node cannot transmit at the full channel rate
It needs a central coordinating node
questions.explain: The drawbacks are wasted collision slots, idle slots, slot time spent even after a collision could have been detected, and clock sync. A single active node can transmit continuously at the full rate, and the protocol is highly decentralized. Those are strengths.

questions.q: In slotted ALOHA, a single active node can transmit continuously at the full rate of the channel.
questions.explain: With no other node transmitting, every slot it uses succeeds, so it gets the full rate R. This is one of slotted ALOHA's strengths.

questions.q: What does CSMA stand for?
questions.explain: Carrier sense multiple access: listen before transmitting.

questions.q: In simple CSMA, what does a node do if it senses the channel busy?
choices: Transmits anyway and relies on collision detection
Defers its transmission
Transmits with probability p in the next slot
Sends a jam signal
questions.explain: Simple CSMA listens before transmitting. If the channel is idle, the node sends the whole frame. If it is busy, the node defers. The human analogy is "don't interrupt others."

questions.q: Why can collisions still happen with carrier sensing?
choices: Nodes only sense the channel at slot boundaries
Carrier sensing works only on wireless links
Propagation delay means a node may not yet hear another node's transmission that has just started
Nodes ignore the channel state after a backoff
questions.explain: A signal takes time to travel along the medium. A distant node can sense the channel idle and start sending before the other node's transmission reaches it. Distance and propagation delay affect how likely collisions are.

questions.q: In CSMA without collision detection, a collision wastes the entire packet transmission time.
questions.explain: Without collision detection, the colliding nodes keep sending their whole frames, so the full transmission time is lost. CSMA/CD fixes this by aborting.

questions.q: How does CSMA/CD improve on simple CSMA?
choices: It removes collisions entirely
It gives each node its own time slot
It detects collisions within a short time and aborts the colliding transmissions, so less channel time is wasted
It lets a central controller schedule transmissions
questions.explain: Collisions are still possible, but they are detected quickly and the transmissions are aborted. That reduces the time wasted per collision. The human analogy is the polite conversationalist.

questions.q: Collision detection is about as easy on wireless links as on wired links.
questions.explain: Collision detection is easy on wired media and difficult on wireless. That is why Ethernet uses CSMA/CD and 802.11 uses CSMA/CA.

questions.q: In Ethernet CSMA/CD, what does an adapter send after aborting a transmission because it detected another transmission while sending?
questions.explain: It aborts, sends a jam signal, and then enters binary (exponential) backoff.

questions.q: In Ethernet's binary exponential backoff, after the 1st collision, from which set is K chosen at random?
questions.explain: After the mth collision, K is chosen from {0, 1, ..., 2^m − 1}. For m = 1 that is {0, 1}.

questions.q: In Ethernet CSMA/CD, after a frame's 3rd collision, how many different values of K can the adapter choose from?
questions.explain: K is drawn from {0, 1, ..., 2^3 − 1} = {0, ..., 7}, which has 8 values.

questions.q: In Ethernet CSMA/CD, after a frame's 4th collision, what is the longest the adapter can wait before going back to sensing the channel? (Answer in bit times.)
questions.explain: For m = 4, K is in {0, ..., 15}. The wait is K·512 bit times, so the most is 15 × 512 = 7680 bit times.

questions.q: A 10 Mbps Ethernet adapter picks K = 3 during backoff. How long does it wait, in microseconds?
questions.explain: At 10 Mbps one bit time is 0.1 µs. The wait is K·512 = 1536 bit times, and 1536 × 0.1 µs = 153.6 µs.

questions.q: Why does Ethernet's backoff interval grow as a frame suffers more collisions?
choices: To give the frame higher priority over newer frames
To keep the slot clocks synchronized
So the adapter has time to recompute the CRC
Repeated collisions suggest heavy contention, and spreading retransmissions over a wider random range makes another collision less likely
questions.explain: More collisions mean a longer backoff interval. A larger set of possible K values spreads the contending nodes apart in time, which lowers the chance that they pick the same retransmission time.

questions.q: In the Ethernet CSMA/CD algorithm, what does an adapter do if it senses the channel busy when it has a frame ready?
choices: Waits until the channel is idle, then transmits
Immediately enters binary exponential backoff
Sends a jam signal
Drops the frame
questions.explain: Step 2: if the channel is idle, start transmitting. If it is busy, wait until it is idle, then transmit. Backoff happens only after a collision aborts a transmission.

questions.q: How do random access MAC protocols behave under low and high load?
choices: Inefficient at low load; efficient and fair at high load
Efficient at low load, since a single node can fully use the channel; collision overhead at high load
Efficient at both low and high load
Inefficient at both low and high load
questions.explain: Random access lets a lone node use the whole channel, but collisions eat capacity when many nodes contend. Channel partitioning is the opposite. Taking-turns protocols try to get the best of both.

questions.q: What are taking-turns MAC protocols trying to achieve?
choices: Zero overhead and zero latency
Dividing the channel into fixed frequency bands
Letting nodes transmit whenever they sense the channel idle
The best of both worlds: efficient, fair sharing at high load and full use by a single node at low load
questions.explain: They aim for partitioning's efficiency and fairness at high load and random access's efficiency at low load. Nodes take turns, but nodes with more to send can take longer turns.

questions.q: In polling, how is it decided which node transmits?
choices: A centralized controller invites the other nodes to transmit in turn
Nodes pass a token from one to the next
Each node senses the channel and transmits when it is idle
Each node has a fixed time slot
questions.explain: A centralized controller (master) polls the client nodes one at a time. Polling is typically used with "dumb" devices, and Bluetooth uses it.

questions.q: Which of these are concerns with polling?
choices: Polling overhead
Latency
Single point of failure (the master)
Collisions between client devices that answer at the same time
Needs carrier sensing, which is hard on wireless
questions.explain: The concerns are overhead from the poll messages, latency while waiting to be polled, and the master as a single point of failure. Only the polled device transmits, so clients don't collide, and no carrier sensing is needed.

questions.q: In token passing, what is the single point of failure?
choices: The centralized controller
The token
The node with the most data
The slot clock
questions.explain: A control token is passed from node to node in order, and a node transmits only while it holds the token. If the token is lost or corrupted, nobody can transmit. The other concerns are token overhead and latency.

questions.q: In token passing, what does a node do when it receives the token and has nothing to send?
choices: Holds the token until it has data
Discards the token
Passes the token on to the next node
Broadcasts a jam signal
questions.explain: The token is passed explicitly from one node to the next in order. A node transmits only while holding it, so a node with nothing to send passes it along.

questions.q: Which of these use a taking-turns MAC protocol?
choices: Bluetooth
FDDI
Token ring
Ethernet (CSMA/CD)
802.11 (CSMA/CA)
questions.explain: Bluetooth uses polling, and FDDI and token ring use token passing. Ethernet and 802.11 use random access protocols.

questions.q: In a cable access network, what does CMTS stand for?
questions.explain: The CMTS sits at the cable headend and connects the cable network to the ISP.

questions.q: Which multiple access techniques does a DOCSIS cable access network combine?
choices: FDM (frequency division)
TDM (time division)
Random access
Token passing
questions.explain: DOCSIS uses FDM for its upstream and downstream channels and TDM minislots upstream. Some slots are assigned, and modems contend for others by random access with binary backoff.

questions.q: Why don't the downstream cable channels need a contention mechanism?
choices: Downstream channels use carrier sensing
A single CMTS is the only transmitter into the downstream channels
Each home has its own dedicated downstream wire
Downstream frames are polled one at a time
questions.explain: Downstream is broadcast over multiple FDM channels (up to 1.6 Gbps each), but only the CMTS transmits into them, so senders never contend. Upstream, many modems share the channels.

questions.q: In DOCSIS, what does the downstream MAP frame do?
choices: Assigns upstream minislots to cable modems for an interval [t1, t2]
Carries the TV channel lineup
Maps IP addresses to MAC addresses
Tells modems which downstream frequency to tune to
questions.explain: The CMTS sends a MAP frame downstream that assigns upstream minislots for the coming interval. Modems then send their upstream data frames in their assigned minislots.

questions.q: In DOCSIS, how does a cable modem request upstream time slots?
choices: It waits to be polled by the CMTS
It holds a token passed among the modems
It always has a fixed dedicated upstream slot
It sends request frames by random access (binary backoff) in certain contention minislots
questions.explain: Requests for upstream slots (and some data) are sent by random access in selected minislots, using binary backoff after collisions. The CMTS then assigns slots through the MAP frame.
